consensus_summary: The pearl symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or salvation/Christ) as a treasure of supreme worth, for which one should surrender everything (Matt 13:45-46); secondary senses include sacred truth not to be profaned (Matt 7:6), the glorified entrance to the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:21), the church/believer purchased by Christ, and a negative sense of luxury/ostentation (1 Tim 2:9; Rev 17-18).
book_summary: The pearl is 'the one complete light': via the Hebrew peninim (KJV 'rubies'), wisdom and the virtuous bride are priced above pearls, and the pearl itself is identified with the full moon (keseh, 'fulness,' linked by wordplay to 'throne' and 'time appointed'), the governor of the appointed times; the one-pearl gates of the city are the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
consensus_core_identification: Pearl = the Kingdom of Heaven / salvation (or Christ) as the treasure of supreme worth, worth everything to obtain.
book_core_identification: Pearl = the full moon as the 'one complete light,' governor of the appointed times, and by extension wisdom/the bride priced above pearls — the one-pearl gate being the King's-gate entry.
boundary_disagreement: The book shifts the pearl's primary corpus from Matthew 13 and Matthew 7 to Proverbs 3:15/31:10 (peninim rendered 'rubies'), Psalm 81:3, Job 26:9, and Psalm 104:19, adding wisdom texts and lunar/calendar texts the consensus never treats as pearl passages, while retaining Revelation 21:21 but reclassifying its one-pearl gates as full-moon imagery rather than generic kingdom glory.
material_contradiction: The consensus identifies the pearl as the Kingdom of Heaven/salvation/Christ (an abstract or personal referent of supreme worth); the book identifies it as a concrete celestial object — the full moon governing the appointed times — with wisdom/the bride as the associated valuation. Pearl-as-full-moon and pearl-as-kingdom cannot both be the referent of the same symbol in the same sense; the book acknowledges the common teaching and supplants it with the lunar identification.
rationale: Both readings agree pearls connote supreme preciousness, but the book's minimum core is a replacement identification: the pearl is the full moon (keseh), the 'one pearl' of the night sky, tied by Hebrew wordplay to the appointed times and to the one-pearl gates. No consensus response or alternative includes a lunar or calendrical referent. The book explicitly notes the common view (kingdom/church) as what is 'commonly taught,' positioning its own reading as a different identification rather than a refinement of the kingdom's boundary. Rev 21:21 is shared but reclassified, making the extension relation partial reclassification while the core is contradicted/replaced.
strongest_objection: One could argue NOVEL rather than DIVERGENT: the book's lunar reading may be intended as complementary symbolism (the moon governing appointed times as an image of entry into the kingdom at the King's gate), not a denial that the parable's pearl means the kingdom; the identification is absent from consensus more than it strictly contradicts it. Additionally, the printed verses do support wisdom-above-pearls (given the peninim gloss) and the one-pearl gates, so the citation judgment could arguably be stronger than partial for that portion.
